data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["The expert's representation is continuous, associative, and high-dimensional; the checklist is discrete, rule-based, and low-dimensional.","The expert's representation is implicit and updated through experience; the checklist is explicit and updated through deliberate revision.","The expert can handle novel cases by analogy; the checklist can only apply pre-specified rules."],"overturn_conditions":["If the checklist is proven to be non-lossy or to encode all relevant features.","If empirical evaluation shows the panel outperforms the expert on complex, non-checklist-friendly tasks.","If the expert's intuition is shown to be systematically biased in ways the checklist corrects."],"shared_structure":["Both the expert and the checklist are representations of task-relevant knowledge.","Both can be evaluated against objective outcomes.","Both are subject to error, but the sources and types of error differ."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_002","SRC_001"],"transfer_claims":["From information theory: a lossy compression cannot fully reconstruct the original signal; thus, the checklist's output is necessarily degraded relative to the expert's internal model.","From expertise research (Dreyfus): experts rely on holistic pattern recognition, not rule-following; checklists force a non-expert mode of cognition that is intrinsically limited."]},"claim":"Against the claim: a trained non-expert panel using an explicit checklist will, on average, underperform a single domain expert for tasks with objectively verifiable outcomes, because the checklist is a lossy compression of the expert's tacit knowledge, and the panel's application of it introduces a new class of errors (misinterpretation, rule ambiguity) not present in expert intuition. The panel's apparent reliability gain may be an artifact of evaluating on narrow, checklist-friendly tasks.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the checklist is not lossy\u2014if it captures all decision-relevant features\u2014then the non-expert panel has access to the same information as the expert.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the panel's aggregation cancels out the misinterpretation errors, the panel may still outperform the expert.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert's intuition is systematically biased in ways the checklist is not, the checklist's lossiness may be a feature, not a bug.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Expert intuition is the product of pattern recognition over a vast internal representation of cases and outcomes. This representation is necessarily richer than any checklist that can be externalized. The checklist is a bottleneck: it can only encode a subset of the expert's decision-relevant knowledge. When non-experts apply this bottlenecked representation, they introduce errors from misreading or misapplying rules. The expert, by contrast, has direct access to the full representation. The checklist's apparent success on objective tasks may be because those tasks are simple enough to be captured by the lossy compression; on complex tasks, the lossiness will dominate.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
